title: Installing Python
objectives: Explain what an installer does to your machine
Check which Python you have with `python3 --version`
Compare two versions part by part
Say what pip and a virtual environment are for

screens.prose: Ana downloads `python-3.12.4.pkg` from python.org and runs it. A minute later the installer says it has finished. To tidy up, she wants to delete the installer from `Downloads`.

state.caption: Her disk after the install, simplified: real folder names vary by system

screens.question: Will `python3` still run after she deletes the installer?

options.text: Yes: Python now lives in a folder of its own
No: Python lives inside the installer
options.why: You treated the installer as the program. It is a package that copies Python out into its own folder.

options.text: Only until she restarts the machine
options.why: You expected the deletion to bite after a restart. The copied files sit in their own folder, so a restart changes nothing.

hints.text: Where is `python3` once the installer has finished?
It sits in `Programs/Python 3.12`, not in `Downloads`.
Deleting the installer removes only the package Python arrived in.

feedback.correct: The installer is only the delivery. Python stays where it was copied.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at where `python3` sits after the installer has run.

explain.text: You found `python3` in a folder of its own, away from `Downloads`. The installer was the box it came in. Binning the box leaves Python where it is.

screens.prose: The installer is a package. Running it unpacks three things: the `python3` program, `pip3`, which fetches extra libraries, and `lib`, a folder of ready-made code.
screens.question: Tap every item the installer created on Ana's disk.

hints.text: Which of these existed before the installer ran?
Everything the installer made sits under this folder, the folder included.

feedback.correct: One new folder and the three things inside it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap the new folder and everything in it, and nothing else.

byKey.with-pkg: You tapped the installer too. Your browser downloaded that file; the installer only unpacked from it.
byKey.no-folder: You tapped the three pieces but not their folder. The installer made `Python 3.12` to hold them.
byKey.d-dl-pkg: Your browser downloaded the installer. It did not create itself.
byKey.d-pr: `Programs` was there before. The installer only added a folder inside it.
byKey.d-dl: `Downloads` was there before, and the installer leaves it alone.
byKey.d: The disk was there before. Tap only what is new.

explain.text: You tapped a new folder and its three items. Copying a program into a folder like this is the heart of installing. Most installers also record where that folder is, so the terminal can find `python3`.

screens.prose: Copying a program into a folder of its own, ready to run, is **installing**. To check it worked, Ana opens a new terminal window. She asks Python for its **version**: three whole numbers, called major, minor and patch.
screens.question: Ana's course needs Python 3.10 or newer. Is her 3.12.4 new enough?

options.text: Yes: minor 12 comes after minor 10
No: its last number, 4, is below 10
options.why: You lined up the 10 with the patch. In 3.10 the 10 is the minor number, so compare it with 12.

options.text: Cannot tell, because 3.10 has no patch number
options.why: You looked for a patch in 3.10. A missing patch means any patch at all: 3.10.0 or later.

hints.text: Both versions start with 3. Which number comes next in each?
The middle number of Ana's version is 12.
Compare the minor numbers: 12 against 10.

feedback.correct: Same major, and minor 12 is past minor 10.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the parts up: major with major, minor with minor.

explain.text: You compared 3 with 3, then 12 with 10. The major numbers tie, so the minor numbers decide. 3.12.4 is newer than any 3.10.

screens.prose: Two lab machines report their versions. The major and minor numbers match. Only the patch differs.
screens.question: What separates machine B's Python from machine A's?

options.text: Seven more rounds of bug fixes, and no new features
Several new language features
options.why: You read the last number as the biggest change. New features arrive with a new minor number. A patch only fixes bugs.

options.text: Nothing: both are Python 3.11
options.why: You stopped reading at 3.11. The patch numbers differ, so B has had fixes that A lacks.

hints.text: Which of the three numbers differs?
Only the patch moves, from 2 to 9.
Patch releases fix bugs in a minor version. They add nothing new to the language.

feedback.correct: Same language, fewer bugs on machine B.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the part that differs, then recall what that part counts.

explain.text: You found that only the patch differs, 2 against 9. Patches fix bugs inside one minor version. A script that runs on one runs on the other.

screens.prose: On her Mac, Ana first types the shorter command, then the longer one.
screens.question: What do the two replies tell her?

options.text: Python is installed, under the command name `python3`
The install failed and must be run again
options.why: You trusted the first reply alone. The second command answers, so Python is there under the name `python3`.

options.text: She has two Pythons, and one is broken
options.why: You read the error as a second, broken Python. Only one command answered: `python` simply names nothing on her machine.

hints.text: One of the two commands worked. Which?
This row shows a real version.
On a Mac or Linux machine the command is usually `python3`. On Windows it is often `py` or `python`.

feedback.correct: The program is there. Only its command name differs from what she typed first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the second reply before deciding.

explain.text: You read both replies, not just the first. `python` names no program on her Mac, but `python3` does. Use the name that answers with a version.

screens.prose: Ana's Mac came with a Python of its own. She now has two, and asks each one its version.
screens.question: Which Python is newer?

options.why: You read the versions as decimals, so 3.9 looked bigger than 3.12. Each part is a whole number, and minor 12 comes after minor 9.

options.text: Neither: both are Python 3
options.why: You stopped at the major number. Both are 3, so the minor numbers decide: 12 against 9.

hints.text: Is 3.12 a decimal number, or two whole numbers joined by a dot?
Compare the minor numbers: 9 and 12.
Minor versions count up 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12. So 3.12 came out three releases after 3.9.

feedback.correct: Minor 12 comes three releases after minor 9.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the minor numbers as whole numbers.

byKey.old: You read 3.9 and 3.12 as decimals, where 0.9 beats 0.12. Versions are not decimals: minor 12 is three releases after minor 9.

explain.text: You compared 9 and 12 as whole numbers. As decimals 3.9 looks bigger, but a version is not a decimal. 3.12 came out years after 3.9.

screens.prose: Every comparison you made used the same rule. Compare the major numbers first; if they tie, the minor numbers; if those tie, the patch. Each part is a whole number: $$\text{major}\,.\,\text{minor}\,.\,\text{patch}$$
screens.question: Put these versions in order, oldest at the top.

hints.text: All four have major 3. Sort by the minor number.
The minor numbers are 8, 9, 10 and 12. The patch numbers do not matter here.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sort by the middle number, read as a whole number.

byKey.v10: You placed 3.10 too early, as if it were the decimal 3.1. Its minor number is 10, after 9.
byKey.v12: You placed 3.12 too early, as if it were the decimal 3.12 below 3.9. Its minor number is 12, the largest here.

explain.text: You sorted on the minor numbers: 8, 9, 10, 12. The big patch numbers, 10 and 14, did not count, because the minor numbers already differ.

screens.prose: Here is the whole install, in the order that works on any machine. One step matters on Windows only.
screens.question: Put the steps in order, first at the top.

lines.text: Download the installer for your system from python.org
Open the installer. On Windows, tick **Add python.exe to PATH** on its first page
Click Install and wait until it says it has finished

hints.text: You cannot open an installer before it is on your disk.
The check comes last, in a terminal window opened after the install.
Download, open and tick, install, new window, check.

feedback.correct: Download, open, install, new window, check.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step needs the one before it to have happened.

byKey.s4: You opened the terminal before the install had finished. A window opened too early may not know where Python went.
byKey.s5: You checked the version too early. The check only means something once Python is installed and a new window is open.

explain.text: Each step needs the previous one: you cannot open what you have not downloaded. The new terminal window comes after the install, because a window opened earlier may not see it. We find out why in a later lesson.

screens.prose:
Python's own `lib` has nothing good for tables of prices. The pandas library has, and **pip** fetches it. Ana types this while her terminal is in her `backtest` folder:

```bash
python3 -m pip install pandas
```
screens.question: Tap the folder that pandas ends up in.

hints.text: pip adds a library to the Python that ran it.
The command began with `python3`, the program in this folder.
Libraries live in that Python's `lib` folder.

feedback.correct: pip copied pandas into the `lib` folder of the Python that ran it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. pip installs into the Python that ran it.

byKey.d-an-bt: You expected pandas in the folder Ana was standing in. pip installs into the Python that ran it, wherever the terminal is.
byKey.d-pr-py: Close: it goes inside this Python, but into its library folder.
byKey.d-pr-py-p: pip did the fetching, but the library is stored with the other libraries.

explain.text: You picked the `lib` folder of the Python that ran pip. `python3 -m pip` means: this Python, run your pip. So pandas is shared by every script this Python runs, wherever they are.

screens.prose:
Ana has two backtests. The old one needs pandas 1.5; the new one needs pandas 2.2. One Python folder holds one pandas. So in each project she runs:

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
```

That makes a **virtual environment**: a folder `.venv` holding a private Python for that project.
screens.question: Why does this end the clash?

options.text: Each project installs into its own `.venv`, so each keeps its own pandas
A virtual environment makes the backtests run faster
options.why: You took the venv for a speed-up. It changes where libraries are kept, not how fast code runs.

options.text: It upgrades both projects to the newest pandas
options.why: You expected one shared upgrade. The point is the opposite: each project keeps the version it was written for.

hints.text: How many copies of pandas does the tree show?
Each project has a `.venv` of its own.
pip run from inside a project's venv installs into that `.venv` only.

feedback.correct: Two private folders, two versions, no clash.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at where each pandas sits in the tree.

explain.text: You saw two `.venv` folders, each with its own pandas. A virtual environment is a private Python per project. Installing into one leaves the other alone.

screens.prose: Ana's team will backtest a moving-average signal with a library that needs Python 3.10 or newer. Five machines report their versions.
screens.question: Tap the version of every machine that can run the backtest.

hints.text: Read the minor number of each version.
These two have minor numbers 9 and 8.
Minor 10 or more qualifies: 12, 10 and 11. Minor 9 and 8 do not.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep every version whose minor number is 10 or more.

byKey.decimal: You kept all five, reading 3.10 as the decimal 3.1. Then 3.9 and 3.8 look new enough, but their minor numbers, 9 and 8, are below 10.
byKey.no-ten: You left out 3.10.14. The library needs 3.10 or newer, and 3.10 itself counts.
byKey.r1c1: You kept 3.9.6. Its minor number, 9, is below 10.
byKey.r3c1: You kept 3.8.10. Its patch is 10, but its minor number is 8.

explain.text: You kept the minor numbers 12, 10 and 11, and dropped 9 and 8. The patch of 3.8.10 is a decoy: the minor number decides first. Two machines need a newer Python before they can join in.

ideas: An installer copies a program into a folder of its own; afterwards the installer itself can go.
`python3 --version` reports major, minor and patch, and you compare them from the left as whole numbers.
pip installs libraries into the Python that runs it, and a virtual environment gives each project its own.

formula.name: Reading a version
formula.note: Compare part by part, as whole numbers, from the left.

summary.trap: Reading 3.9 and 3.12 as decimals makes the older version look newer.

options.why: You read 3.9 as a decimal, bigger than 3.12. Minor 9 comes before minor 12.
You let the patch, 9, decide. The minor numbers differ first: 12 beats 11.
You stopped at the first version with a two-digit minor. 12 is larger still.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the minor numbers as whole numbers.

explain.text: All four have major 3, so the minor numbers decide: 10, 9, 12 and 11. The largest is 12, so 3.12.0 is newest. Its patch of 0 does not matter.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The minor number is the middle one.

byKey.patch: You gave the last number. That is the patch; the minor is the middle one.
byKey.major: You gave the first number. That is the major; the minor is the middle one.

explain.text: A version reads major, minor, patch. In 3.11.4 the middle number is 11.

quiz.prose: Ana wants the requests library, which fetches web pages, in her Python.
quiz.question: Which command installs it?

options.text: `python3 -m pip install requests`
`python3 install requests`
options.why: You asked Python itself to install. That is pip's job, so the command needs `-m pip`.

options.text: `python3 --version requests`
options.why: You reached for the version check. `--version` only reports which Python you have.

feedback.correct: This Python runs its pip, which installs requests.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Libraries are installed by pip.

explain.text: `python3 -m pip` runs the pip that belongs to this Python. `install requests` tells it what to fetch. The library lands in this Python's folder.

quiz.prose: Two of Ana's projects each have their own `.venv` folder.
quiz.question: She installs pandas 2.2 inside the first project's venv. What happens to the second project?

options.text: Nothing: its venv keeps whatever it had
It gets pandas 2.2 as well
options.why: You pictured one shared library folder. Each venv has its own, so the second is untouched.

options.text: Its pandas is removed
options.why: You expected the two to fight over one copy. Separate folders mean neither touches the other.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about where pip put pandas.

explain.text: pip installed into the first project's `.venv` only. The second project has its own folder of libraries. That separation is the reason to use a venv.
